questions.title: How does the sequence-level importance ratio $s_i(	heta)$ in GSPO avoid the high-variance problem that plagues token-level ratios in GRPO?
questions.question_body: In GRPO each token gets an importance weight $w_{i,t}(	heta)$ based on a single sample from the old policy. I understand that this leads to large variance especially for long responses, but I still don’t see why replacing the per‑token weight with a single sequence‑level weight normalized by length eliminates this variance. Can you explain the intuition behind length normalization and how it stabilizes the gradient?

questions.title: Why does the advantage $	ilde{A}_i$ in GSPO use groupwise mean and std versus a value model?
questions.question_body: Both GRPO and GSPO compute $	ilde{A}_i$ as a standardized relative reward within a group of $G$ responses to the same query. Why is this preferable to training a separate value network? Does standardizing over a small group always provide an unbiased advantage estimate, or are there scenarios where it might be biased?

questions.title: Can you derive step by step how the gradient of GSPO (Eq. (10)) simplifies to Eq. (11)?
questions.question_body:
I see the general form of $
abla_	heta 	ext{E}[s_i 	ilde{A}_i] = 	ext{E}[s_i 	ilde{A}_i 
abla_	heta 	frac{1}{|y_i|}	frac{	ext{d}}{	ext{d}	heta}	au]$ but I’m missing how the log‐likelihood terms combine and why the division by $|y_i|$ appears. A detailed derivation would help clarify how the sequence‐level importance ratio ends up inside the log‐derivative.

questions.title: What would happen if we directly applied GRPO’s clipping range $ ig[1-ho,1+ho ig]$ to GSPO’s normalized importance ratio $s_i(	heta)$?
questions.question_body: The paper mentions that GSPO’s clipping ranges differ in order of magnitude from GRPO’s because their importance ratios are defined differently. If I adopt GRPO’s typical clipping parameters (e.g., $ho=0.2$) for GSPO, would I observe instability or diverging gradients? How sensitive is GSPO to its clipping threshold?

questions.title: Why is only one group required per query in GSPO? Would increasing $G$ beyond 4 improve performance or stability?
questions.question_body:
The experiments use $G=4$ regardless of model size or answer length. Intuitively, a larger group might provide more accurate advantage estimates and better exploration, but it also increases data generation cost.
What is the theoretical trade‑off here, and under what circumstances would I need to increase $G$?

questions.title: `GSPO‑token` seems identical to `GSPO` when all token advantages are equal – does `GSPO‑token` add any practical benefits beyond expressiveness?
questions.question_body: `GSPO‑token` introduces token‑level advantages while still normalizing by sequence likelihood. In practice, have you observed any gains from using token‐specific advantages (e.g., with multi‑turn dialogues) compared to the simpler `GSPO`? Are there scenarios where token‐level advantages hurt stability?

questions.title: How does GSPO circumvent expert‑activation volatility in Mixture‑of‑Experts models without Routing Replay?
questions.question_body:
Mixture‑of‑Experts models suffer from large changes in activated experts after a policy update, which makes token‑wise importance ratios unstable.
Because GSPO uses only sequence likelihoods, it claims to be robust to expert activation changes.
Could you quantify how much activation change actually affects $s_i(	heta)$ versus $w_{i,t}(	heta)$, and why this matters for stability?

questions.title: Why is using inference engine probabilities safe for GSPO but not for GRPO or PPO?
questions.question_body:
"GSPO is more tolerant of precision discrepancies between training and inference engines, so we can reuse inference logits".
Could you elaborate on what kinds of precision errors would break token‑level algorithms but leave GSPO unaffected? Are there edge cases where even GSPO would still be vulnerable?
